name: Treaty at Camp Barbour, on the San Joaquin River (1851), unratified California treaty N
aka: Treaty N of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 4 set apart 'forever' for the sole use and occupancy of the sixteen tribes a district running from the Chowchilla river to the Kaweah river (the first of the Four Creeks), crossing the Fresno, San Joaquin and Kings rivers, with the privilege of hunting and gathering in the country east of it to the Sierra Nevada.
Article 5: five hundred head of beef cattle and two hundred and sixty sacks of flour in each of the years 1851 and 1852, divided by the agent according to the tribes' numbers.

Article 6: clothing, cloth, blankets, iron and steel in each of the two years after ratification, and in the first year brood mares, milch cows, work cattle, mules, ploughs, seed and tools as joint tribal property.

Article 7: a farmer with two assistants, a carpenter, a blacksmith, three principal school teachers and assistant teachers, paid by the United States for five years and as long after as the President thought advisable, with school houses, shops and dwellings.

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty N in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

breaches.what: Table Mountain Rancheria states that the lands promised to the sixteen tribes in the Treaty of Camp Barbour were never given and that the treaty was never ratified.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Table Mountain Rancheria, Our Story page

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 275 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

plain.promised: A district from the Chowchilla to the Kaweah river set apart forever for sixteen tribes, with hunting and gathering to the Sierra Nevada, plus cattle, flour, clothing, tools, farmers, a blacksmith and school teachers.
plain.happened: The Senate refused to ratify the treaty on July 8, 1852, and kept it secret until 1905. Table Mountain Rancheria says the lands promised were never given.
plain.today: The treaty remains unratified. A 1928 Act let California Indians sue for the promised lands and compensation; the amount finally paid has not been traced. The North Fork Mono Tribe says no one received anything.

nationVoice.summary: The Rancheria's history says the Treaty of Camp Barbour, the second of the 18 treaties, was made on April 29, 1851 with sixteen San Joaquin, Fresno and Kings River tribes including the Chukchansi, Gashowu, Choinumne, Pitcatchi, Dumna, Ketchayi and Posgisa Mono, and that the lands it promised were never given because it was never ratified.

The Tribe says the North Fork Mono were never contacted and so were left off the treaty signings, though the treaty named them to receive what the signers were to get, and that no one received anything; the Tribe remains without federal acknowledgment.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Buena Vista Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; California Valley Miwok Tribe, California; Chicken Ranch Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; Ione Band of Miwok Indians of California; Jackson Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians of California; Middletown Rancheria of Pomo Indians of California; Picayune Rancheria of Chukchansi Indians of California; Santa Rosa Indian Community of the Santa Rosa Rancheria; Santa Rosa Indian Community of the Santa Rosa Rancheria, California; Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, Shingle Springs Rancheria (Verona Tract), California; Table Mountain Rancheria of California; Tule River Indian Tribe of the Tule River Reservation; Tule River Indian Tribe of the Tule River Reservation, California; Tuolumne Band of Me-Wuk Indians of the Tuolumne Rancheria of California.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

In Article 3 the signing tribes gave up their claims to other lands; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).
Audit 2026-11-08: promises corrected against treaty N as printed in Heizer (1972), the treaty text at https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366/files/arfs003-001.pdf.
Status set to broken on 2026-11-08 under Jordan's rule: never ratified, but the land was taken and a finding documents it. The never-ratified breach stays so the map labels it.
